events.excerpt: Last week at GitHub Universe, we announced our new Git storage architecture, capable of handling thousands of writes per second with reads that scale on demand. Through internal testing, we’ve demonstrated the ability to support 5,000 concurrent agents working on a repository, sending 7,200 pushes per second to a repo, all while serving read traffic with consistently low latency. This new architecture is the foundation for GitHub to support agentic development for hundreds of millions of developers, and we’ve been building it underneath GitHub while it keeps running. Over the past year, agents changed what a busy repository looks like on GitHub. In our first post in this series, we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation Git storage architecture: minimize coordination, and decouple storage from compute. In our last post , we covered the bridge: moving 99.99999% of repositories into Azure, scoping the write quorum to individual references, and standing up virtual replicas backed by Azure Blob Storage. We also left off with an observation: very little of a write needs to be ordered. Git objects are immutable and named by their contents, meaning two writers can store them at the same time without agreeing on anything. The part of a push that needs agreement is the ref
events.headline: Inside GitHub’s new Git storage architecture

events.excerpt: AI agents do more than generate answers. They search for information, query databases, write and test code and take action. Each of those steps relies on a CPU, with agents moving between GPU reasoning and CPU execution throughout a task. As businesses put more agents to work, AI factories need CPUs that can execute those steps quickly and support many agents at once, all within the limits of available power. What this means: AI infrastructure providers need to support more agents without making each one wait longer to get work done. And critically, AI factories are power limited. This means operators need to choose infrastructure that maximizes the work done for every watt. Why it matters: NVIDIA Vera delivers both fast agent performance and high capacity per watt within a single CPU. That gives providers one CPU for a range of agent workloads, rather than having to mix and match fast and dense x86 parts to balance speed and capacity. The data that proves it: In a 100-megawatt data center comparison, NVIDIA found that a single Vera CPU performs better than the fastest x86 CPU and the most energy-efficient x86 CPU. Vera delivers industry-leading agent speed while enabling 1.6x more agents per watt versus the fastest x86 CPU. Vera delivers 2x faster agent speed with leading energy
events.headline: Vera Delivers the Best of Both Worlds: Highest Throughput and Fastest Agents

events.excerpt: AI Agents now act on the web for millions of people. To a Site, an Agent can take many forms. It may be indistinguishable from a human user carrying out a task, or it might look like one visitor carrying many Users. This removes the ability for the Site to recognize, serve, and hold accountable the user or users behind the Agent, and causes the Site to face the costs when something goes wrong. This post argues that in order for Sites to maximize the access they provide to Agents, the ecosystem must develop new mechanisms to preserve the relationship between Sites and Users. Traditionally, in Security and Fraud Prevention, that requires three things: Identity, Reputation, and Accountability, allowing Sites to answer: Is the person acting being truthful about who they are? Is that person trustworthy? events.excerpt: Walraswap: equilibrium-based decentralized exchange integrating external AMM liquidity This is an announcement of the research article with the same title and a brief informal intro for ethresear.ch. A classic approach to tackling MEV in decentralized exchanges on Ethereum is to enable a mechanism that receives trade orders during a block interval and settles all the swaps in a batch following a fairness criterion. It is an old problem. I imagine that an informed reader might feel somewhat skeptical. Thoughts of this kind were expressed in 2014 in this Reddit post . CoW Swap, UniswapX, 1inch’s Fusion, Sorella’s Angstrom, and Propellerheads’ Turbine have all tackled the problem using batch trading in one way or another. Walraswap started in 2023 at Flashbots, independently of the previous and closely related work by Ramseyer, Goyal, Goel, and Mazières: Augmenting Batch Exchanges… and SPEEDEX . The central feature in common: we treat the DEX problem from the point of view of the theory of equilibrium for an exchange economy with n tokens. events.excerpt: At a glance Formal methods for everyday software. PDD Kit helps you turn your intent into a formal spec, then proves the code your agent writes for every input and uses tests where a proof can’t reach. It takes formal methods beyond niche, specialist work to engineers without a formal methods background and to everyday applications, like the full-stack web app shown here. Exhaustive line-by-line human review can become difficult to scale as AI agents generate increasingly large amounts of code. The plan is supposed to be the contract between you and a coding agent, but nothing actually forces the agent to follow it. The tests it writes usually check what it built, rather than what you asked for. PDD Kit makes the agent keep the plan. It works with you to turn your intent into a formal specification in Verus (opens in new tab) , proves the agent’s code meets that spec for every input, and falls back to tests where a proof can’t reach. We tried it on a full-stack web app. Inside GitHub Next’s Chopin (opens in new tab) , we used PDD Kit to formally verify the login logic of Pet Store, a Rust (opens in new tab) storefront. events.headline: Formally verifying agent-written full-stack web apps with PDD Kit

events.excerpt: Larger models, longer contexts and agentic applications are increasing GPU memory pressure while supply tightens and prices rise — a trend expected to continue through the near term. NVIDIA works closely with memory partners to rapidly adopt the latest memory technologies. NVIDIA was first to adopt HBM3e and HBM4 technologies into an accelerated computing stack. But the approach isn’t to simply pack more memory onto the GPU. It’s full-stack codesign. NVIDIA intentionally designs GPUs, CPUs, networking, storage and software together to get more useful work out of memory at every layer of the AI factory. That matters because an AI factory runs on a memory and storage hierarchy. GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM) is the fastest, most expensive and most contested tier — with model weights and KV cache competing for limited capacity. Below it sit CPU memory, local SSDs and shared storage, each trading speed for more capacity at a lower cost per bit. How much useful work a byte does depends on how well the whole hierarchy is used: shrinking what must be stored, placing it on the right tier and bringing it back to the GPU before it’s needed. Byte for byte, NVIDIA makes the most efficient use of memory at every layer — and the results show it. From NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra to the Vera Rubin p
events.headline: More Performance From Every Byte: How Full-Stack Codesign Solves AI’s Memory Challenge

events.excerpt: Accessibility work often lives in issue trackers, contribution guidelines, audit reports, team knowledge, and conversations with users. When that information has no predictable home, people who encounter a barrier must search for it, and maintainers lose context as contributors and project ownership change. An ACCESSIBILITY.md file, now visible on repository overview pages, gives a project one durable place to explain its accessibility goals, contributor expectations, supported environments, known limitations, and process for reporting barriers. GitHub makes accessibility statements easier to find GitHub now recognizes the ACCESSIBILITY.md file in the repository’s root, .github/ directory, or docs/ directory. A repository can also inherit a statement from its organization’s .github/ repository. For public repositories, maintainers can add or propose a statement from Insights > Community Standards using a concise starter document. GitHub’s community health files help people understand how a project works: Contribution guidelines explain how to propose changes Codes of conduct establish expectations for participation Security policies explain how to report vulnerabilities Recognizing ACCESSIBILITY.md gives accessibility information a dedicated place alongside that guidance. events.excerpt: Abstract This standard defines a proxy that coordinates execution sessions by temporarily caching a program and its associated calldata in transient storage. The proxy forwards the cached program to a fixed implementation through DELEGATECALL and uses a handler flag to control whether subsequent reentrant invocations are dispatched. The program remains unchanged throughout an execution session, while the cached calldata is replaced on each accepted invocation. This enables a single implementation to coordinate callback-driven execution using different programs and calldata without deploying a new contract for each execution. Motivation Many advanced execution strategies require dynamically changing execution logic, particularly when interacting with external contracts that invoke callbacks during execution. Traditionally, dynamically changing the execution logic of a contract may require deploying a new contract containing the desired runtime code. This introduces deployment costs, including contract creation and code-deposit costs. Flash Loan Proxy separates the execution program from the implementation responsible for interpreting it. Instead of deploying a new contract for each program, callers provide the program as calldata. The proxy temporarily caches the program and forwa

events.excerpt: Proposal Type : Ratification Executive Summary This Ratification vote adds an Upgrade Authority Transfer policy to the Governing Policies section of the Standard Rollup Charter. It sets out how a Chain Governor may request that upgrade authority for its chain be transferred from the Security Council to an address of its choosing, so the chain can manage upgrades itself or through a third party. Under the policy, the Optimism Foundation confirms a valid request and publishes a public notice on the Governance Forum. After a mandatory 30-day notice period, the Security Council is directed to execute the transfer. Once the transfer is executed, the chain ceases to be a Standard Rollup. This is a non-fork upgrade. It changes Charter language only: no smart contract or node software changes are required, and this proposal executes no onchain transactions. Motivation The Standard Rollup Charter defines how a chain becomes a Standard Rollup, including authorizing the Security Council to perform upgrades. It does not define how a chain leaves. Today, a Chain Governor that wants to take back upgrade authority has no published path, and any transfer would require ad hoc governance action. This gap matters for three reasons: Predictability for Chain Governors. Handing upgrade authority to th

events.excerpt: Important Optional but highly recommended upgrade. v2.5.1 is a hardening & maintenance release. No protocol fork is activated, and operators can upgrade in-place. v2.5.1 carries robustness improvements across the P2P layer, block processing, the transaction pool and the public/admin APIs, together with a handful of API and SDK fixes. Most changes are internal; the user-visible ones are listed below. What's Changed Hardening & Robustness These changes tighten resource bounds and failure handling throughout the node. They do not change consensus rules: every bound is sized above what a valid block can hold under the current 40M block gas limit. Networking : new blocks received from a peer are handed off through a per-peer mailbox instead of being processed on the peer's read loop. Transaction broadcast now uses a single bounded queue and writer per peer. Future-block cache entries are capped per peer and bound to their header. Inbound connection attempts are rate-limited per source (one per 30s for a non-LAN IPv4 address or IPv6 /64 prefix), matching go-ethereum ( #1699 ). Internal consistency fixes in the discv5 topic table. Block decoding : stricter bounds while decoding block headers and bodies (header field widths, total clause count per block). events.excerpt: Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016. The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President ( AS2650 ). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period. The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica , a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications . events.excerpt: Proposal Type: Protocol Upgrade Hi, I’m Andrea Federici, Senior Solutions Engineer at OP Labs. I prepared this proposal in collaboration with Matthew Cruz from the OP Labs team. Neither OP Labs nor I, nor any other entity mentioned, represent or speak on behalf of the Optimism Foundation. Executive Summary Upgrade 21 is an L1 smart contract upgrade for OP Stack chains, shipped in op-contracts/v9.0.0 . It has no hardfork and no activation timestamp: every change is applied through a signed superchain-ops execution on L1. It contains the following changes: ETHLockbox as custody and pause identifier — every chain gets an ETHLockbox that cannot be disabled, and it becomes the only identifier for a chain-specific pause. Chains whose ETH is still in the OptimismPortal have it moved into the lockbox in the upgrade transaction. Chains that already use a lockbox are unchanged. Custom gas token chains get a lockbox but keep custody in the portal. Permissionless deleteProvenWithdrawal — anyone can delete a withdrawal proof whose dispute game resolved in favor of the challenger or was blacklisted. Proofs on valid games are unaffected. OPCM v9.0.0 and StandardValidator — removes the startingAnchorRoot upgrade override, lowers batched-upgrade gas, and adds validator checks for the new lockbox

events.excerpt: Release Notes Node version 11.2.0 is a pre-release version of cardano-node that is not yet recommended for use on mainnet. Its headline change is the move to the new cardano-config library for reading node configuration: the node now understands a versioned configuration "envelope" alongside the existing flat format, and the configuration files published for each network are now in the envelope format. It also extends the gRPC interface, continues the groundwork for the Dijkstra era, Leios and Peras, and fixes several operator-facing bugs. Highlights: New configuration format. Configurations are read through cardano-config . Existing flat configurations still work. The new envelope format ( $schema / Version / MinNodeVersion / Configuration ) is schema-validated. New cardano-node config migrate , cardano-node config schema and cardano-node config resolve subcommands convert, describe and check a configuration. The shipped network configs are now enveloped and cannot be read by nodes older than 11.2 . gRPC over HTTP/2. The gRPC server can now listen on a TCP address/port, in plaintext (h2c) or with TLS ( --grpc-listen-address / --grpc-listen-port , --grpc-tls-* ), instead of only a unix socket. New gRPC methods ReadMempool , WatchMempool and ReadEraSummary , plus server reflection

Abstract Deploying and distributing private smart contracts, confidential L2/Validium state diffs, or permissioned intent payloads across Ethereum’s public P2P and Data Availability (DA) layers currently faces a fundamental metadata bottleneck. Even when contract bytecode or state is symmetrically encrypted, existing Broadcast Encryption (BE) and Attribute-Based Encryption (ABE) schemes require attaching an explicit cleartext header specifying either the authorized recipient indices, covering subsets, or the target access tree. In this post, we propose an architectural framework based on Stealth Attribute-Based Broadcast Encryption (Stealth ABBE) over BLS12-381 ( Zenodo Preprint ) for zero-metadata delivery of private contracts and encrypted state on Ethereum. By reformulating broadcast access control as a homomorphic blind Reed–Solomon decoding problem over 𝔽 256 using carry-free Base-3 packing in exponential ElGamal ciphertexts (𝔾 1 × 𝔾 1 ), Stealth ABBE achieves: O(1) Broadcast KEM Size (24.1 KiB amortized): Fits comfortably inside a single EIP-4844 blob (~19% of one 128 KiB blob) regardless of the total participant count N . Zero Visible Headers or Revocation Lists (0 Bytes): Access policies, cohort rosters, and revocation states are algebraically absorbed into the non-system
events.headline: Stealth ABBE over BLS12-381: Zero-Metadata Broadcast of Private Contracts & Encrypted State via EIP-4844 Blobs
